# Dependency contracts and lifetime ownership

[← All question groups](../index.md) · `dotnet-di-solid` · **C# & .NET Runtime** · Catalog level: senior

<p>Questions come from the preserved source notes. Reframing, assessment intent, senior signals and rubrics are editorial interpretations, not verified model answers or universal interviewer expectations. Follow-ups and the combined production exercise are agent additions. Reading this bank creates no learning record, score, completion or review schedule.</p>

## Start with one representative question

[S01-Q032](#S01-Q032)

<p>Compare Dependency Inversion, Inversion of Control and Dependency Injection using one small design. What distinguishes the ideas and how do they relate?</p>

## One group objective and observable capabilities

<p>Design dependency relationships that remain valid across change and service lifetime boundaries.</p>

<ul>
<li>Distinguish DIP, IoC and DI in the same design.</li>
<li>Trace instance ownership and identify a captive dependency.</li>
<li>Assess SOLID contracts and refactor one recurring change pressure.</li>
</ul>

**Prerequisites**

No catalog prerequisite. Establish the terms and scenario assumptions in the foundation questions before progressing; a published lesson is not evidence that you know them.

<p>Dependency direction explains who relies on which contract; construction and lifetime explain who supplies and retains its implementation. SOLID checks then ask whether that relationship survives replacement or a new requirement without breaking callers.</p>

### S01-Q035 · Foundation

<p>Explain the SOLID principles with concrete production-oriented examples. For one principle, show the change pressure and how you would assess a proposed design.</p>

**Source:** [S01-Q035](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q035)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S01-Q035](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q035)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> Explain the SOLID principles with production examples.

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Retain the full set of principles but go deeper on one relevant example. An example should explain responsibility, contract or dependency effects rather than just label classes.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Use design principles to reason about a concrete change.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Clearly mark proposed examples as hypothetical unless they are genuine experience; do not invent incidents, team outcomes or measured benefits.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Connects each principle to a meaningful design concern and traces one change in detail.</li>
<li>Considers a simpler alternative and the evidence needed to justify extra abstractions.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Reciting the acronym or declaring that more interfaces automatically means better design.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>When would applying your proposed abstraction create more cost than benefit?</li>
</ul>

</details>

### S01-Q032 · Foundation

<a id="S01-Q037"></a>

<p>Compare Dependency Inversion, Inversion of Control and Dependency Injection using one small design. What distinguishes the ideas and how do they relate?</p>

**Source:** [S01-Q032](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q032) · [S01-Q037](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q037)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Separate the design principle, control relationship and construction technique in your explanation. Show their relationship without treating the three names as synonyms.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Reason about dependency direction independently of container configuration.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Use a hypothetical application service and replaceable dependency; include IoC from the broader source question as well as the DIP/DI comparison.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Draws dependencies and object construction for the same concrete example.</li>
<li>Explains whether the design goal is met and how a change would test that claim.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Claiming that registering services in a container alone proves good dependency direction.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>Could your example retain its design goal without a DI container?</li>
</ul>

</details>

### S01-Q033 · Mechanism

<p>How do Transient, Scoped and Singleton lifetimes affect object creation, reuse and cleanup? Trace two requests resolving the same service registration.</p>

**Source:** [S01-Q033](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q033)

<p class="scope-note">Version-sensitive scope: state the actual runtime/framework/provider and check official documentation before making technical claims. This question bank does not certify current behavior, product defaults or performance results.</p>

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S01-Q033](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q033)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> Explain `Transient`, `Scoped`, and `Singleton` lifetimes.

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Follow the instances each consumer receives and the scope in which they live. Connect lifetime to state ownership rather than simply reciting three definitions.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Predict service-instance behavior from registration and scope boundaries.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Name the DI container, framework version and scope setup; consult official documentation for actual resolution and disposal rules.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Traces instance identity across resolutions and requests with an explicit scope.</li>
<li>Explains how shared mutable state or resource ownership affects the lifetime choice.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Assuming scoped always means one HTTP request in every hosting context.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>How would you establish a suitable scope in a background worker?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S01-Q036"></a>

### S01-Q036 · Mechanism

<p>How do Liskov Substitution and Interface Segregation address different contract problems? Use an example to show which concern you are diagnosing.</p>

**Source:** [S01-Q036](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q036)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S01-Q036](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q036)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> Compare Liskov Substitution and Interface Segregation.

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Examine what consumers can rely on when using an abstraction. Compare substitutability with the breadth of a contract instead of merging both into “small interfaces.”</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Distinguish behavioral compatibility from unnecessary contract coupling.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Use a hypothetical caller and implementations; state valid inputs, expected outputs and obligations before labeling a violation.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Demonstrates the caller expectation at risk for each principle.</li>
<li>Explains a targeted redesign and a contract check without introducing unrelated patterns.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Calling every large interface a substitution violation without showing a failed behavioral contract.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>Which tests would reveal that a replacement implementation breaks a caller?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S01-Q038"></a>

### S01-Q038 · Application

<p>Show a concrete violation of the Open/Closed Principle and propose a refactor. Which expected changes should become easier, and what should remain stable?</p>

**Source:** [S01-Q038](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q038)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S01-Q038](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q038)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> Give an example of violating Open/Closed Principle and how you would refactor it.

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Identify the change that repeatedly forces edits, then assess an extension boundary. The task needs before-and-after reasoning rather than a pattern name.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Refactor a recurring change pressure with bounded complexity.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Use a small hypothetical module; state the expected family of changes and preserve existing behavior instead of promising no future edits anywhere.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Shows the affected code or design and a regression-check plan.</li>
<li>Explains the abstraction’s cost and a case where the original simple implementation is preferable.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Interpreting the principle as a ban on all modifications or solving unknown future changes in advance.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>What new requirement would challenge the boundary you selected?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S01-Q034"></a>

### S01-Q034 · Failure cases

<p>What can go wrong when a longer-lived service retains a shorter-lived dependency? Trace the dependency’s use across the shorter lifetime boundary.</p>

**Source:** [S01-Q034](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q034)

<p class="scope-note">Version-sensitive scope: state the actual runtime/framework/provider and check official documentation before making technical claims. This question bank does not certify current behavior, product defaults or performance results.</p>

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S01-Q034](../../sources/01-csharp-dotnet.md#q034)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> What problems occur when a longer-lived service captures a shorter-lived dependency?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>A captive dependency is a dependency retained beyond the lifetime its design intended. Investigate the resulting state and ownership problem, not only the registration syntax.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Diagnose a lifetime mismatch and defend a repair.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Name the container, versions, scope and resource ownership; consult official documentation before claiming the container detects or prevents the problem.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Shows a concrete use after the intended boundary and its observable risk.</li>
<li>Compares a lifetime change with an explicit scope boundary and checks cleanup and concurrency.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Treating successful resolution as proof that dependency lifetimes are safe.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>How would you test the repair under overlapping requests or jobs?</li>
</ul>

</details>

## Combined production exercise — agent-added

<p>A hypothetical singleton coordinator uses a data-access dependency and gains a new processing policy. Draw construction and dependency direction, trace two overlapping jobs and resource cleanup, and identify any lifetime mismatch. Propose a bounded refactor and contract tests rather than adding interfaces everywhere.</p>

## Short rubric — use only with an actual attempt

**Basic answer**

<p>Explains the terminology and lifetimes with a consistent instance trace.</p>

**Senior answer**

<p>Defends ownership, substitution and extension boundaries while comparing a simpler repair.</p>

**Still needs evidence**

<p>Successful container resolution or a list of SOLID names does not establish safe lifetimes or good contracts.</p>
